headline: “Peace of mind” is an old Chinese compound, and the same spelling has a twin reading with rendaku.
Soap is, in Chinese, “stone lye”.
A men's suit may be tied to English “civil clothes”, Savile Row or Cheviot — and the kanji say “wide back”.
A balloon is a “wind ship”, and the word seems to have been coined in Japan around 1860.
さすが is “sasuga ni” with its last syllable dropped, and the reason for its kanji is still an open question.
“Fool” is spelled “horse + deer”, but those characters were fitted to the sound — probably an allusion to an old Chinese saying.
“Shortage” is, in Chinese, just “not enough”.
Midnight is the “middle of the night”.
“Regrettable” is “lingering” plus “concern”, and appears in texts from the late 1500s.
The chair began as a seat for court officials and came to mean the wooden seat of a Zen priest.
Katakana is “partial kana” — the same 片 as in 方, “direction”.
“Up and down” came over from Chinese as a ready-made compound — and じょうげ is likely its first reading.
Noisy is “making noise” plus an adjective-making ending.
A porter is a clipped “bellboy”, while a boy is just an English boy.
“Proactive” is the “positive pole” with an adjective-forming suffix.
“Trouble” is spelled with kanji that are only ateji — so where the word came from is an open question.
“The world” began as a translation of a Sanskrit term for “region or part of the world”.
A birthday is a “birth day”, with ひ voiced to び.
“To differ” began as “roads that cross” — dated to 974.
A volcano's crater is a “fire mouth” — and the same two characters have more than one reading.
Furigana are kana you “assign” to a character; the word dates from 1813.
Massage reached Japanese through English and French, and began in an Arabic word for “feel, touch”.
Fabric or dough is “raw ground” — and the word first meant bare, unlacquered wood.
ひとこと is the native reading; the same spelling also has Chinese-derived readings, one likely borrowed first.
The month after next can be broken down two ways, and references disagree on which is right.
“Healthy” began as the fundamental force of the cosmos, until it was confused with a word for recovery.
A name is “name” plus “front” — and its look-alike in English is a coincidence.
Banzai is a mixed reading: the second part kept an older Chinese sound while the first took a newer one.
“Before” began as “what lies just in front of your hand”.
A rocket and a locket share one katakana spelling.
